result: Experiment 1 demonstrated that imposed sensorimotor delays progressively destabilized standing balance. Sway velocity variance increased with delay magnitude (reaching maximum at 400 ms: 21.08 ± 15.41 [°/s]²), and all participants exceeded virtual balance limits when delays were ≥200 ms.
evaluation: Claims C20-C36 and C95 provide converging evidence from Experiment 1 with appropriate statistical analysis (main effect of delay, p<0.001) and clear quantitative measurements. The data show systematic increases in sway variability and decreases in time within balance limits as delays increased, with critical threshold around 200 ms.

result: Participants learned to balance with a 400 ms imposed delay through training over 5 days (100 min total). Sway velocity variance decreased by ~80% and time within balance limits increased by 51%, with time constants of ~28-33 min. Learning was partially retained after 3 months.
evaluation: Claims C37-C52 provide detailed quantitative evidence of learning with exponential fits, statistical comparisons, and retention data. The results demonstrate that humans can learn to control balance with total delays of 500-560 ms (400 ms imposed + 100-160 ms physiological), exceeding the predicted critical delay of 300-340 ms from computational models.

result: Vestibular-evoked muscle responses (measured via EVS-EMG coherence, gain, and cross-covariance) were attenuated by imposed delays before training, with responses decreasing for delays ≥200 ms. After training, vestibular responses partially recovered, with significant increases in cross-covariance amplitudes for delays ≥200 ms (p<0.05).
evaluation: Claims C53-C69 provide comprehensive vestibular testing data with appropriate frequency-domain and time-domain analyses. Statistical tests show significant delay × learning interactions (p<0.001), and planned comparisons demonstrate recovery of vestibular responses after training. The partial recovery supports the interpretation that the nervous system updated its sensorimotor estimates.

result: Perceptual testing showed that imposed delays triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion, with detection probability increasing from 4% at 50 ms to 100% at 350 ms. After training, psychometric functions shifted rightward, with detection thresholds increasing from 147 ± 21 ms to 192 ± 40 ms post-learning (p=0.032).
evaluation: Claims C73-C81 provide perceptual data with appropriate psychometric analysis using Bayesian curve fitting. The rightward shift in thresholds after training indicates that larger delays were needed to evoke perceptions of unexpected motion, supporting the interpretation that participants learned to associate delayed feedback with self-generated commands.

result: Experiment 3 tracked the time course of responses to transient 200 ms delays. Vestibular coherence attenuated with a time constant of 1.5 ± 0.6 s (63.2% attenuation), and perceptual detection occurred at 3.4 ± 1.8 s on average, corresponding to ~90% reduction in coherence and 73% reduction in gain.
evaluation: Claims C82-C94 provide detailed temporal analysis linking vestibular attenuation, sway variability, and perceptual detection. The time-frequency analysis appropriately characterizes the dynamics of vestibular response changes, and the temporal alignment between vestibular attenuation and perceptual detection supports the mechanistic interpretation.

result: Learning generalized across delays despite training only at 400 ms. Vestibular responses and sway behavior improved at multiple untrained delays (20-500 ms), suggesting the nervous system broadly updated its control rather than specifically recalibrating to the 400 ms delay.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C128-C129 correctly identify that training was only at 400 ms, yet improvements occurred at other delays. This generalization is well-documented in the vestibular and perceptual testing data (C63-C64, C68-C69, C80-C81), supporting the inference of broad sensorimotor recalibration.

result: The main mechanistic conclusion is that the nervous system learns to accommodate balance sensorimotor delays by causally linking delayed whole-body sensory feedback (initially interpreted as imposed motion) to self-generated balance motor commands, involving sensorimotor recalibration rather than simple sensory reweighting.
evaluation: Claims C7, C10, C25, C103, C148 state the main mechanistic interpretation, which is supported by the convergence of vestibular recovery (C60-C64), perceptual threshold shifts (C76-C78), and behavioral improvements (C41-C42). The inference that this involves recalibration (C113-C115) is justified by the partial return of vestibular responses and generalization across delays, which cannot be explained by simple gain reduction.

result: Prior literature establishes that errors increase with feedback delays, the brain can learn to expect delays up to 430 ms in upper-limb tasks, standing balance has inherent delays of ~100-160 ms, and computational models predict balance cannot be stabilized with delays >300-340 ms.
evaluation: Claims C11-C15 are appropriately cited background claims that establish the context for the study. The citations appear relevant and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in motor control and balance research.

result: Prior work demonstrates that novel sensorimotor relationships initially disrupt performance but can be learned through recalibration, including vestibular feedback manipulations, delayed touch perception, and cerebellar mechanisms for updating sensorimotor predictions.
evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C116-C120, C124-C126 provide appropriate citations to relevant prior work on sensorimotor adaptation, vestibular recalibration, temporal recalibration, and neural mechanisms. These establish the theoretical framework for interpreting the current findings.

result: Discussion of control models: optimal controllers can theoretically stabilize standing with large delays but decline with accelerations; intermittent control may be a solution when delays rule out continuous control; sensory reweighting predicts gain decreases with delays.
evaluation: Claims C105-C112 appropriately cite relevant computational modeling literature and discuss alternative control strategies. The authors acknowledge (C110) that their study did not explicitly test these different controllers, which is an appropriate limitation statement.

result: The authors discuss interpretational challenges: while vestibular and perceptual changes may reflect balance errors, it is unclear what specific component of standing behavior is attributable to prediction errors versus other factors like control policy changes or movement kinematics.
evaluation: Claims C132-C137 appropriately acknowledge limitations in causal interpretation. The authors correctly note (C133) that they cannot definitively separate prediction error effects from other factors, and suggest (C134-C135) alternative explanations with appropriate citations. This represents appropriate scientific caution.

result: Clinical implications: The standing balance system can be trained to accommodate larger delays than predicted, which may benefit clinical populations with increased neural delays due to aging or disease. Training with delays might enable targeted rehabilitation.
evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are supported by the experimental findings showing learning beyond predicted limits. However, C141 is speculative about clinical applications without supporting data from clinical populations. The translation from healthy young adults to clinical populations requires validation.

result: Limitation: The experimental manipulation delayed whole-body motion relative to ankle torques, but did not delay all somatosensory signals (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, cutaneous receptors), which may have created sensory conflicts affecting learning.
evaluation: Claims C142-C144 appropriately identify a methodological limitation. The authors correctly note that their manipulation selectively delayed some sensory feedback but not others, which could have influenced the results. This is an important caveat for interpretation.

result: Methods: 46 healthy adults participated across three experiments using a robotic balance simulator with imposed delays. Vestibular responses were measured using EVS-EMG coherence, gain, and cross-covariance. Perceptual testing used button presses to detect unexpected motion.
evaluation: Claims C149-C168 describe the methods with appropriate detail. The robotic system, vestibular stimulation, and analysis techniques are well-established methods cited appropriately (C153-C154, C167-C168). Sample sizes are clearly stated for each experiment.

result: General principle: Human standing balance relies on self-motion estimates that accommodate for inherent sensory and motor delays, enabling detection of unexpected movements and corrective responses.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 state general principles about balance control that are well-established in the field and form the conceptual foundation for the study. These are appropriately characterized as knowledge claims.

result: After training, vestibular contributions partially returned to baseline levels, with every participant showing significant biphasic muscle responses at all delays post-training, and cross-covariance amplitudes significantly larger for delays ≥200 ms.
evaluation: This result is already covered in the vestibular testing result above but emphasizes the completeness of recovery (C61 - every participant showed responses). The statistical evidence (C63-C64) strongly supports partial recovery.
